1.1: From my grandfather Verus I learned good morals and how to govern my temper.
1.2: From the reputation and memory of my father, modesty and a manly character.
1.3: From my mother, piety and generosity, and abstaining not only from evil deeds but even from evil thoughts; and further, simplicity in my way of living, far removed from the habits of the rich.
1.4: From my great-grandfather, not to have attended public schools, and to have had good teachers at home, and to know that on such things a man should spend generously.
1.5: From my tutor, to be neither of the Green nor of the Blue party at the games in the Circus, nor a supporter of either the Parmularius or the Scutarius at the gladiators' fights; from him too I learned to endure hard work, and to want little, and to work with my own hands, and not to meddle in other people's affairs, and not to be ready to listen to slander.
1.6: From Diognetus, not to busy myself with trivial things, and not to believe what was said by miracle-workers and conjurers about incantations and the driving away of demons and such things; and not to breed quails for fighting, nor to give myself up passionately to such things; and to put up with frank speech; and to have become familiar with philosophy; and to have been a pupil, first of Bacchius, then of Tandasis and Marcianus; and to have written dialogues in my youth; and to have wanted a plank bed and a skin, and whatever else of the kind belongs to the Greek discipline.
1.7: From Rusticus I received the impression that my character needed improvement and discipline; and from him I learned not to be led astray into the rivalry of the sophists, nor into writing on speculative matters, nor into delivering little speeches of moral exhortation, nor into showing myself off as a man who practises much discipline, or does kind acts in order to make a display; and to keep away from rhetoric, and poetry, and fine writing; and not to walk about the house in my outdoor clothes, nor to do other things of the kind; and to write my letters simply, like the letter which Rusticus wrote from Sinuessa to my mother; and, with respect to those who have offended me by words or done me wrong, to be easily disposed to be pacified and reconciled, as soon as they have shown a readiness to be reconciled; and to read carefully, and not to be satisfied with a superficial understanding of a book; nor to agree hastily with those who talk too much; and I owe it to him that I became acquainted with the discourses of Epictetus, which he passed on to me from his own collection.
1.8: From Apollonius I learned freedom of will and unwavering steadiness of purpose; and to look to nothing else, not even for a moment, except reason; and to be always the same, in sharp pains, at the loss of a child, and in long illness; and to see clearly in a living example that the same man can be both most resolute and yielding, and not irritable in giving his instruction; and to have had before my eyes a man who clearly regarded his experience and his skill in explaining philosophical principles as the least of his merits; and from him I learned how to receive from friends what are regarded as favours, without being either humbled by them or letting them pass unnoticed.
1.9: From Sextus, a kindly disposition, and the example of a household governed in a fatherly way, and the idea of living in keeping with nature; and dignity without affectation, and to look carefully after the interests of friends, and to put up with ignorant people, and those who form opinions without thinking: he had the ability to adapt himself readily to everyone, so that conversation with him was more pleasant than any flattery; and at the same time he was most highly respected by those who spent time with him: and he had the ability both to discover and to arrange, in an intelligent and methodical way, the principles necessary for life; and he never showed anger or any other passion, but was entirely free from passion, and also most affectionate; and he could express approval without noisy display, and he had much knowledge without showing it off.
1.10: From Alexander the grammarian, to refrain from finding fault, and not to scold in a reproachful way those who used any barbarous or ungrammatical or strange-sounding expression; but skilfully to bring in the very expression which ought to have been used, by way of answering, or confirming, or joining in an inquiry about the thing itself, not about the word, or by some other fitting suggestion.
1.11: From Fronto I learned to observe what envy and duplicity and hypocrisy are like in a tyrant, and that, generally, those among us who are called Patricians are rather lacking in paternal affection.
1.12: From Alexander the Platonist, not to say to anyone, often or without need, or to write in a letter, that I have no time; nor continually to excuse the neglect of the duties required by our relationship with those we live with, by pleading urgent business.
1.13: From Catulus, not to be indifferent when a friend finds fault, even if he should find fault without reason, but to try to restore him to his usual frame of mind; and to be ready to speak well of teachers, as is said of Domitius and Athenodotus; and to love my children truly.
1.14: From my brother Severus, to love my family, and to love truth, and to love justice; and through him I came to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dion, Brutus; and from him I received the idea of a state in which there is the same law for all, a state governed with regard to equal rights and equal freedom of speech, and the idea of a kingly government which respects above all the freedom of the governed; I learned from him also consistency and unwavering steadiness in my regard for philosophy; and a disposition to do good, and to give to others readily, and to cherish good hopes, and to believe that I am loved by my friends; and in him I observed no concealment of his opinions about those whom he condemned, and that his friends had no need to guess what he wanted or did not want, but it was quite plain.
1.15: From Maximus I learned self-control, and not to be led astray by anything; and cheerfulness in all circumstances, and in illness too; and a fair blend in the moral character of sweetness and dignity, and to do what was set before me without complaining. I observed that everybody believed that he thought as he spoke, and that in all he did he never had any bad intention; and he never showed amazement or surprise, and was never in a hurry, and never put off doing a thing, nor was he perplexed or dejected, nor did he ever laugh to disguise his irritation, nor, on the other hand, was he ever quick-tempered or suspicious. He was in the habit of doing acts of kindness, and was ready to forgive, and was free from all falsehood; and he gave the impression of a man who could not be turned aside from what is right, rather than of a man who had been improved. I observed, too, that no man could ever think that he was despised by Maximus, or ever venture to think himself a better man. He also had the art of being humorous in a pleasant way.
1.16: In my father I observed gentleness of temper, and unchangeable resolution in the things which he had decided after due deliberation; and no vanity about the things which men call honours; and a love of work, and perseverance; and a readiness to listen to those who had anything to propose for the common good; and unwavering firmness in giving to every man according to what he deserved; and a knowledge, gained from experience, of the occasions for vigorous action and for relaxation. And I observed that he had overcome all passion for boys; and he considered himself no more than any other citizen; and he released his friends from all obligation to dine with him or to attend him as a matter of course when he went out, and those who had failed to go with him, because of some urgent circumstance, always found him the same. I observed too his habit of careful inquiry in all matters for deliberation, and his persistence, and that he never stopped his investigation through being satisfied with the appearances which first present themselves; and that his disposition was to keep his friends, and not to be soon tired of them, nor yet to be extravagant in his affection; and to be content on all occasions, and cheerful; and to foresee things a long way off, and to provide for the smallest without display; and to check at once popular applause and all flattery; and to be always watchful over the things which were necessary for the administration of the empire, and to be a good manager of expenditure, and to endure patiently the blame which he got for such conduct; and he was neither superstitious with respect to the gods, nor did he court men by gifts or by trying to please them, or by flattering the people; but he showed moderation in all things, and firmness, and never any mean thoughts or actions, nor love of novelty. And the things which contribute in any way to the comfort of life, and of which fortune gives an abundant supply, he used without arrogance and without apology; so that when he had them, he enjoyed them without affectation, and when he did not have them, he did not miss them. No one could ever say of him that he was either a sophist or a flippant, home-bred slave or a pedant; but everyone acknowledged him to be a man mature, complete, above flattery, able to manage his own and other men's affairs. Besides this, he honoured those who were true philosophers, and he did not reproach those who pretended to be philosophers, nor yet was he easily led by them. He was also easy in conversation, and he made himself pleasant without any offensive affectation. He took reasonable care of his body's health, not as one who was greatly attached to life, nor out of concern for his personal appearance, nor yet in a careless way, but so that, through his own attention, he very seldom needed the art of the physician, or medicine, or external applications. He was most ready to give, without envy, to those who had any particular ability, such as eloquence or knowledge of the law or of morals, or of anything else; and he gave them his help, so that each might enjoy a reputation according to his merits; and he always acted in keeping with the institutions of his country, without showing any affectation of doing so. Further, he was not fond of change, nor unsteady, but he loved to stay in the same places, and to occupy himself with the same things; and after his attacks of headache he came at once, fresh and vigorous, to his usual occupations. His secrets were not many, but very few and very rare, and these only about public matters; and he showed prudence and economy in putting on public spectacles, in the construction of public buildings, in his gifts to the people, and in such things, for he was a man who looked to what ought to be done, not to the reputation which a man gets by his acts. He did not bathe at unusual hours; he was not fond of building houses, nor particular about what he ate, nor about the texture and colour of his clothes, nor about the beauty of his slaves. His clothes came from Lorium, his villa on the coast, and from Lanuvium generally. We know how he behaved to the toll-collector at Tusculum who asked his pardon; and all his behaviour was like that. There was nothing in him harsh, nor unforgiving, nor violent, nor, as one might say, anything carried to the point of sweating; but he examined all things one by one, as if he had plenty of time, and without confusion, in an orderly way, vigorously and consistently. And what is recorded of Socrates might be applied to him: that he was able both to abstain from, and to enjoy, those things which many are too weak to abstain from, and cannot enjoy without excess. But to be strong enough both to bear the one and to be sober in the other is the mark of a man who has a perfect and invincible soul, such as he showed in the illness of Maximus.
1.17:
To the gods I owe it that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good companions, good relatives and friends, nearly everything good. Further, I owe it to the gods that I was not hurried into any offence against any of them, though I had a disposition which, had the opportunity arisen, might have led me to do something of the kind; but, through their favour, circumstances never came together to put me to the test. Further, I am thankful to the gods that I was not brought up any longer with my grandfather's mistress, and that I kept the flower of my youth, and that I did not prove my manhood before the proper time, but even put it off; that I was placed under a ruler and father who was able to take all pride away from me, and to bring me to understand that it is possible for a man to live in a palace without needing guards or embroidered clothes, or torches and statues, and such-like show; but that it is in such a man's power to bring himself very close to the way of life of a private citizen, without being for this reason either meaner in thought or more careless in action with respect to the things which must be done for the public interest in a way that befits a ruler. I thank the gods for giving me such a brother, who was able by his moral character to rouse me to watchfulness over myself, and who at the same time pleased me by his respect and affection; that my children have not been stupid or deformed in body; that I did not make more progress in rhetoric, poetry, and the other studies, in which I might perhaps have become completely absorbed if I had seen that I was making progress in them; that I made haste to give those who brought me up the positions of honour which they seemed to want, without putting them off with the hope that I would do it some other time, since they were then still young; that I knew Apollonius, Rusticus, Maximus; that I received clear and frequent impressions about living according to nature, and what kind of life that is, so that, as far as it depended on the gods, and their gifts, and help, and inspirations, nothing prevented me from living according to nature straight away, though I still fall short of it through my own fault, and through not heeding the warnings of the gods and, I might almost say, their direct instructions; that my body has held out so long in such a way of life; that I never touched either Benedicta or Theodotus, and that, after falling into passionate love, I was cured; and, though I was often out of humour with Rusticus, I never did anything I had cause to regret; that, though it was my mother's fate to die young, she spent the last years of her life with me; that, whenever I wished to help anyone in need, or on any other occasion, I was never told that I did not have the means to do it; and that I myself never had the same need, to receive anything from another; that I have such a wife, so obedient, so affectionate, and so simple; that I had plenty of good teachers for my children; and that remedies have been shown to me in dreams, among others against spitting blood and dizziness...; and that, when I became inclined to philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of any sophist, and that I did not waste my time on writers of histories, or on solving syllogisms, or busy myself investigating appearances in the heavens; for all these things require the help of the gods and of fortune.

Among the Quadi, at the Granua.
